# `silk/text/segmentation`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Grapheme cluster, word and sentence boundaries (UAX #29), with data from Unicode 18.0.0.

## When to use
Use [`graphemes`](#graphemes) or [`GraphemeCursor`](#GraphemeCursor) to find user-perceived characters, for example to move
a text cursor or to truncate text. Use [`words`](#words) for word selection and [`sentences`](#sentences) for
sentence selection. Use `silk.text.line_break` to find where a line can wrap.

## Details
The functions implement the default (untailored) rules of UAX #29 revision 49. They take a
`string` and report byte offsets into it. A boundary list is appended to a caller-owned list. It
is sorted and includes 0 and the text's byte length once each, even for empty text. The scans
use constant extra storage and look at each scalar a bounded number of times.

## Gotchas
The rules are not tailored for a language. Word boundaries do not split Thai, Lao, Khmer,
Myanmar, Chinese or Japanese text, and sentence boundaries do not know abbreviations.

## Examples
### Count the user-perceived characters of a text
```silk
import silk.collections.list { List }
import silk.core.effect { Effect }
import silk.mem.allocator { Allocator, OutOfMemoryError }
import silk.text.segmentation

pub effect fn main() -> i32
  ! OutOfMemoryError {
  let mut allocator = Allocator.systemAllocatorProvider()
  let mut boundaries = List<usize>.make()
  // "e" with a combining acute accent, a family emoji joined with ZWJ, and "x".
  run segmentation.graphemes("e\u{301}\u{1f468}\u{200d}\u{1f469}\u{200d}\u{1f467}x", &mut boundaries)
    |> Effect.provideMut<Allocator>(&mut allocator)
  if boundaries.length() - 1 != 3 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `segmentation` with `import silk.text.segmentation as segmentation`.

## `GraphemeCursor`

```silk
pub struct GraphemeCursor
```

A forward cursor over the extended grapheme clusters of one text. It does not allocate.

### When to use
Use a `GraphemeCursor` to step through user-perceived characters one at a time, without a list
of boundaries. Use [`graphemes`](#graphemes) to get all boundaries at once.

### Details
Make the cursor with [`GraphemeCursor.make`](#GraphemeCursor.impl.make) and pass the same text to each call of
[`GraphemeCursor.next`](#GraphemeCursor.impl.next). The cursor implements the default extended grapheme cluster rules of
UAX #29 for Unicode 18.0.0, including the GB9c rule for Indic conjuncts and the emoji rules.

### Gotchas
The cursor keeps only a byte offset and rule state. Passing a different text to a later call
gives meaningless boundaries; it does not trap.

<a id="GraphemeCursor.impl.next"></a>

### Method `next`

```silk
pub fn next(self: &mut Self, text: string) -> usize
```

Moves to the next extended grapheme cluster boundary in `text` and returns its byte offset.

#### Details

The first call returns the end of the first cluster, never 0. After the last cluster, each
call returns `text`'s byte length. For empty text, each call returns 0.

<a id="GraphemeCursor.impl.nextBytes"></a>

### Method `nextBytes`

```silk
pub fn nextBytes(self: &mut Self, text: &[u8]) -> usize
```

Moves to the next extended grapheme cluster boundary in the UTF-8 bytes `text` and returns
its byte offset.

#### When to use

Use `nextBytes` in a scan that holds UTF-8 bytes rather than a `string`. Use
[`GraphemeCursor.next`](#GraphemeCursor.impl.next) otherwise.

#### Details

The result is the same as [`GraphemeCursor.next`](#GraphemeCursor.impl.next) for the same text. An ill-formed byte counts
as U+FFFD and moves one byte.

<a id="nextGrapheme"></a>

## `nextGrapheme`

```silk
pub fn nextGrapheme(text: string, start: usize) -> usize
```

Returns the byte offset of the extended grapheme cluster boundary that follows `start` in
`text`.

### Details

`start` must be a cluster boundary, such as 0 or a result of an earlier call. At or past the
end of `text`, the result is `text`'s byte length. The function does not allocate.

### Gotchas

A `start` that is not a cluster boundary is not detected. The scan starts there as if a new
cluster began, so the result can split a cluster.

<a id="graphemes"></a>

## `graphemes`

```silk
pub effect fn graphemes(text: string, output: &mut List<usize>) -> ()
  ! OutOfMemoryError
  ? &mut Allocator
```

Appends the extended grapheme cluster boundaries of `text` to `output`, as byte offsets.

### When to use

Use `graphemes` to count or split user-perceived characters, for example to move a text cursor
or to truncate text without cutting an accent or an emoji from its base.

### Details

The boundaries follow the default extended grapheme cluster rules of UAX #29 for Unicode 18.0.0.
They are sorted and include 0 and `text`'s byte length once each, so empty text gives one
boundary, 0. The number of clusters is the number of boundaries minus 1. The function does not
clear `output`, so clear it first to reuse its storage.

### Errors

- `OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot grow `output`.

<a id="words"></a>

## `words`

```silk
pub effect fn words(text: string, output: &mut List<usize>) -> ()
  ! OutOfMemoryError
  ? &mut Allocator
```

Appends the word boundaries of `text` to `output`, as byte offsets.

### When to use

Use `words` for double-click selection, word counts, or moving a cursor by words.

### Details

The boundaries follow the default word boundary rules of UAX #29 for Unicode 18.0.0. They are
sorted and include 0 and `text`'s byte length once each, so empty text gives one boundary, 0.
Spaces and punctuation are segments of their own: filter the segments that contain letters or
digits to count words. The function does not clear `output`, so clear it first to reuse its
storage.

### Errors

- `OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot grow `output`.

### Gotchas

The default rules do not split Thai, Lao, Khmer, Myanmar, Chinese or Japanese text into words.
Each run of those characters stays one segment.

<a id="sentences"></a>

## `sentences`

```silk
pub effect fn sentences(text: string, output: &mut List<usize>) -> ()
  ! OutOfMemoryError
  ? &mut Allocator
```

Appends the sentence boundaries of `text` to `output`, as byte offsets.

### Details

The boundaries follow the default sentence boundary rules of UAX #29 for Unicode 18.0.0. They
are sorted and include 0 and `text`'s byte length once each, so empty text gives one boundary,
0. A sentence keeps its trailing spaces and closing punctuation. The function does not clear
`output`, so clear it first to reuse its storage.

### Errors

- `OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot grow `output`.

### Gotchas

The default rules do not know abbreviations, so `"Mr. Smith"` has a boundary after `"Mr. "`.
